lesson.summary: Introduction to C: History, Characteristics and Classification
points: Dennis Ritchie developed C at Bell Labs in the early 1970s, building on B in the Unix environment.
C is general purpose, procedural and imperative; it is normally compiled.
Portability needs care with implementation-dependent behavior. Middle-level is an informal classroom label, not an ISO language category.

tasks.prompt: Archive case 6: Is middle-level an official ISO C language category?
choices: Yes, it is a variable type
No; it is an informal teaching description
Yes, it is a compiler mode
tasks.explanation: No; it is an informal teaching description.

tasks.prompt: Archive case 6: Which limitation should a learner recognize?
choices: Compilation alone does not establish program correctness
Every accepted program meets every goal
tasks.explanation: Compilation alone does not establish program correctness.

tasks.prompt: Archive case 6: An archive describes middle-level as a required ISO compiler setting. What should be corrected?
choices: Middle-level is an informal teaching label
It is a built-in C type

tasks.explanation: Middle-level is an informal teaching label.

archive_evidence.history: The C standard describes a language and a library interface. Middle-level is a classroom description rather than a category specified by that standard.
archive_evidence.source: Dennis Ritchie, The Development of the C Language

archive_evidence.history: Unix introduced pipes after McIlroy argued that commands should be able to pass data to other commands. Each small step could then contribute to a larger task.
archive_evidence.source: Dennis Ritchie, The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System

archive_evidence.history: C is general-purpose, procedural and imperative. Middle-level is an informal teaching label. A compiler accepting a program does not prove that it works or runs unchanged everywhere.
archive_evidence.source: GNU C Language Introduction and Reference Manual

archive_evidence.history: General-purpose is about the kinds of tasks a language can express. Procedural is about organizing work into functions. Imperative is about executing instructions that can change state.
archive_evidence.source: GNU C Language Introduction and Reference Manual

archive_evidence.history: The standard describes the language and library. It does not define a middle-level compiler mode or certify that a program meets its goal.
archive_evidence.source: Dennis Ritchie, The Development of the C Language
